newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bank rescue vehicle seeks changes to control.
newsitem.headline: French bank rescue vehicle seeks changes to control.

text.p: A top official of the rescue vehicle set up to sell off the bad assets of Credit Lyonnais called on Friday for an overhaul of its system of control after a report forecast the bank's losses would top 100 billion francs ($16.9 billion).
"We want a complete reorganisation of our system of control," Francois Lemasson, managing director of the Consortium de Realisation (CDR), told afternoon daily Le Monde.
"We need to be changed into a company with a supervisory and management board," he said.

An official close to the CDR said such a move would allow the agency to have independent advisers to "help it make its economic choices and there would be more neutrality. Sales would not be made for administrative-political reasons."

Lemasson's appeal came after the EPFR, the state body charged with overseeing the CDR, said on Wednesday its organisation was "too complex" and fixed contradictory aims of quick asset sales at the best price.
The CDR was set up in 1995 under a government rescue of the state-controlled Credit Lyonnais bank to house mainly bad assets belonging to the bank.
Credit Lyonnais almost collapsed in the early 1990s after an ill-fated expansion spree.
The CDR is charged by the government with selling 190 billion francs of assets belonging to Credit Lyonnais.
The EPFR said this week CDR's total losses from disposing of the assets would hit 100.2 billion francs, not including carrying costs.
Estimates of the losses from the bank's expansion spree during the 1980s that almost triggered its collapse have risen steadily from 14 billion in 1994.

The previous conservative government set the CDR a target of selling 80 percent of its portfolio within five years. This has brought criticism that the agency is selling the assets for bargain-basement prices to meet the time deadline.
There have also been allegations that political influence has been exercised on some of its sales.
Lemasson said the CDR's structure as a defeasance vehicle hurt its ability to get the best price.
The "simple fact that we are set up as a defeasance structure is a handicap to get the best value for assets which we hold," he said.
